name: FENRIS INDUSTRIAL HaulerFrame HX-9 Arm
product_name: Fenris Industrial HaulerFrame HX-9 Heavy Labor Arm
description:
The HaulerFrame HX-9 is a full-arm replacement engineered for sustained heavy labor, built around a dual-hydraulic load-bearing skeleton rated to 3,400N continuous grip and 8,000N peak crush force. The exterior is deliberately utilitarian — matte black polymer housing over industrial steel framing with modular attachment points at the wrist for swappable tool-head interfaces including hook, clamp, magnetic plate, and pry-bar configurations. The hydraulic system is self-contained and designed for replacement in field conditions using standard dock-tech tools without specialist support.

The HX-9 is the workhorse of GLMZ's lakefront cargo docks, Shelf manufacturing floors, and deep-infrastructure construction crews. Fenris sells them in bulk contracts to industrial employers who often subsidize installation costs against worker wages — a practice that labor organizers have loudly criticized as indentured augmentation. Workers who own their HX-9s rather than renting them from employers wear that ownership with considerable pride.
installation_requirements: Full shoulder disarticulation, industrial-grade neural coupler, available at Meridian Prosthetics partner clinics and employer-contracted surgical bays
rejection_risk: Moderate – high mechanical load stress on shoulder socket causes progressive bone-anchor fatigue without regular reinforcement injections
maintenance: Monthly hydraulic pressure check, quarterly tool-head port cleaning, annual socket stress evaluation

cultural_context: On the Shelf docks, a pair of HX-9s is a working person's inheritance — some families pass down well-maintained units across generations, re-socketing them into children who take the same jobs. Labor organizers have made the employer-subsidy-for-indentured-augmentation model a central grievance in three major strikes over the past decade, with mixed results.

story_hooks: A dock foreman is found crushed to death — the only tool capable of that force pattern is an HX-9 running above rated spec, and someone has been modifying units on the floor
A labor organizer is collecting evidence that an employer's subsidized HX-9 units contain hidden firmware that tracks worker location and physiological stress data
A retired dockworker's cherished bilateral HX-9 set was stolen, and they want them back — but the arms have been modified and sold into something far more dangerous
